lines.text: Interior design transforms empty rooms into functional, beautiful, and emotionally resonant living spaces. It encompasses far more than choosing paint colours and cushions — it is the art and science of shaping how people experience the built environment from the inside. A professional interior designer considers spatial planning (how rooms flow and connect), lighting design (natural and artificial), material selection (flooring, wall finishes, fabrics), colour psychology (how colours affect mood and perception), and furniture arrangement (balancing proportion, scale, and comfort). British interior design reflects a distinctive sensibility — layered, collected, and lived-in rather than rigidly coordinated. The quintessential English interior combines antique furniture with contemporary pieces, patterned textiles with plain walls, and personal objects with carefully chosen art. Current British trends include biophilic design (incorporating nature through plants, natural materials, and daylight), Japandi (a fusion of Japanese minimalism and Scandinavian warmth), and maximalism (bold patterns, rich colours, and eclectic layering). Sustainability is increasingly central: reclaimed materials, vintage furniture, low-VOC paints, and locally sourced craftsmanship. The open-plan kitchen-living-dining space has become the default layout for modern British homes, though a counter-trend toward 'broken plan' — using screens, level changes, and furniture to create zones within an open space — is growing. Interior design magazines (Livingetc, Elle Decoration, House & Garden), television programmes (Interior Design Masters, Grand Designs), and social media (Instagram, Pinterest) have democratised design knowledge and aspiration.

lines.text: The living room feels cold and disconnected — we love the space but it doesn't feel like home yet.
lines.name: The living room feels cold and disconnected — we love the space but it doesn't feel like home yet.

lines.text: I can see why. The walls, sofa, and floor are all similar tones of grey — there's no warmth, no contrast, and no focal point. Let's start with a colour palette.
lines.name: I can see why. The walls, sofa, and floor are all similar tones of grey — there's no warmth, no contrast, and no focal point. Let's start with a colour palette.

lines.text: We like calm, natural tones — nothing too bold or trendy.

lines.text: Perfect. I'd suggest a base of warm white walls with a scheme built around natural textures — linen curtains, a jute rug, wooden side tables. Then we introduce warmth through your accent colour — perhaps a deep terracotta or soft sage.
